newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss Re EPS higher on SAFRA deal - paper.
newsitem.headline: Swiss Re EPS higher on SAFRA deal - paper.

text.p: Walter Kielholz, chief executive of Swiss Reinsurance Co, said the sale of France's SAFR to Bermuda-based Partner Re Ltd would lead to an increase in Swiss Re's earnings per share (EPS) of three to four percent.

Kielholz also said in an interview with Swiss business weekly HandelsZeitung that he was optimistic Swiss Re would get closer to its target of a 15 percent Return on Equity (ROE) when 1996 results are announced.
Asked whether Swiss Re's ROE would already hit the targetted 15 percent in 1996, Kielholz told the paper:
"I am optimistic; we will get very close to that."
In 1995 Swiss Re's ordinary net profit rose 54 percent to 1,092 million Swiss francs, or 75 francs per share. The ROE was 12.7 percent.
Swiss Re has forecast another increase in profit of more than 20 percent for 1996, excluding the acquisition of Britain's Merchant and General Re.
A spokesman for Swiss Re confirmed the interview.
Last month Swiss Re said it would sell Societe Anonyme Francaise de Reassurances (SAFR) to PartnerRe after completing the acquisition of SAFR and make a capital gain of 100 million Swiss francs.
SAFR would be spun-off from Swiss Re around the middle of this year when the recently-announced deal is completed.
Swiss Re consolidates SAFR at equity and owns 21.6 percent.
Instead of SAFR, Swiss Re's stake in Partner Re will be raised to 21.8 percent from 11.1 percent and this will be reflected in its group accounts.
"We expect a positive contribution to earnings per share of around three to four percent from this transaction," Kielholz told the weekly.
As part of the deal, Swiss Re initially will buy SAFR shares it does not already own from Assurances Generales de France (AGF) and Athena, a unit of Worms et Cie.
Swiss Re said in February that it intended to buy the 78 percent of SAFR shares it did not already own -- 57 percent from AGF and Athena and 21 percent from the public.
Swiss Re will make a cash tender offer to public shareholders after completing the acquisition of shares from AGF and Athena group.
Kielholz said Swiss Re had not initiated this transaction, but SAFR majority shareholder AGF wanted to pull out of the reinsurance business and was looking for a buyer.
"As SAFR minority shareholder, Swiss Re wanted to hinder that SAFR landed with one of our main competitors," Kielholz said, adding Swiss Re made use of its rights of first refusal.
However, it also became clear that Partner Re, originally purely a catastrophe reinsurer, at the same time was looking to diversify.
Kielholz said Partner Re's success had boosted its equity so it was facing the issue of whether to pay money back to shareholders or acquire a company outside the catastrophe reinsurance business.
"SAFR -- which has no catastrophe cover but good worldwide customer contacts -- offered a unique opportunity to diversify and sell its own insurance through Partner Re," Kielholz said.
